meta: A general leaderboard doesn't grade your work. Write your own AI test in 4 steps: 1. Take about 10 questions from real work. 2. Write down what good looks like. 3. Same test for every AI. 4. Keep it and rerun it.

muc.title: Write your own test for AI
muc.text: Last time, we watched AIs in blind matches in the arena. But a general leaderboard doesn't grade your work. Today, you write the test.

muc.title: Lan's online shop
muc.text: Lan sells traditional dresses online. Every day she asks AI to write product descriptions and reply to customers. The AI at the top of the leaderboard may not be the one that best fits her shop's voice.

muc.title: Take questions from real work
muc.text: Step one: pick about 10 questions from the work you do every week. Not trick puzzles from the internet, but real customer messages, real spreadsheets, real reports.

muc.title: Write down what good looks like
muc.text: Step two: write down what good looks like before you read any answers. For example: correct price, friendly tone, under 100 words. Score each point from 1 to 5.

muc.title: Same test, same measuring stick
muc.text: Step three: give the same test to each AI and grade with the same points. Hide the names if you can, so you're not biased toward the one you like.

muc.title: Keep the test, grade again
muc.text: Step four: save the test. Whenever a new AI comes out, run it again and compare scores. Your ten questions say more about your work than any number in an ad.

muc.title: 5 tasks, 2 AIs
muc.text: Today: write down 5 real tasks you often give AI, each with points to score from 1 to 5. Try them on 2 AIs, then see which one wins at your work.

muc.title: Grading what's hard to grade
muc.text: But some things are harder to grade than right or wrong: is AI honest, is it safe? See you in part 5.
